nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a pattern of length $m$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$ and write $P_k$ for its prefix of length $k$. For every state $q \le m$ and symbol $a < A$, the entry at index $qA + a$ of the transition table of $P$ is the greatest $k \le m$ such that $P_k$ is a suffix of the word $P_q a$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the string-matching transition table

nodes.summary: For every pattern of length $m$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, the cost of computing its transition table is at most $2A(m+1)^3$.
nodes.title: Cost bound for the string-matching transition table

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a pattern of length $m$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$ and write $P_k$ for its prefix of length $k$. This timed computation returns a table of $(m+1)A$ entries in $\{0, \dots, m\}$, stored row by row: for each state $q \le m$ and symbol $a < A$, the entry at index $qA + a$ is found by trying $k = \min(m, q+1)$ and then each smaller value in turn, and is the first $k$ for which $P_k$ is a suffix of…
nodes.title: Transition table of the string-matching automaton

nodes.summary: For every pattern $P$ and text $T$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, the list of shifts returned by the finite-automaton matcher equals the list returned by the naive string matcher.
nodes.title: Correctness of the finite-automaton matcher

nodes.summary: For every pattern $P$ and text $T$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, where $T$ has length $n$, the cost of the finite-automaton matcher on $P$ and $T$ equals the cost of computing the transition table of $P$, plus $2n$, plus the number of shifts the matcher returns.
nodes.title: Exact cost of the finite-automaton matcher

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a pattern of length $m$ and $T$ a text over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$. This timed computation first computes the transition table of $P$, then runs through $T$ starting in state $0$: on reading the $i$-th symbol $a$ of $T$ in state $q$ it moves to the state given by the table entry at index $qA + a$, and if that state is $m$ it reports the shift $i - m$. If $m = 0$, the shift $0$ is also reported…
nodes.title: Finite-automaton string matcher

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a pattern of length $m$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$ and write $P_k$ for its prefix of length $k$. For every word $w$ over this alphabet, the state that the string-matching automaton of $P$ reaches from its start state after reading $w$ is the greatest $k \le m$ such that $P_k$ is a suffix of $w$.
nodes.title: The string-matching automaton tracks the longest matched prefix

nodes.summary: For a pattern $P$ of length $m$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, the string-matching automaton of $P$ is the deterministic finite automaton with states $\{0, \dots, m\}$, input symbols $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, start state $0$, accepting set $\{m\}$, and transition from state $q$ on symbol $a$ given by the entry at index $qA + a$ of the transition table of $P$.
nodes.title: String-matching automaton

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
